entries.title: publish to npm by trusted publishing
entries.body:
Every release now publishes its packages to npm from `release.yml`, so
`npm install -g @amritk/nish` and `npx @amritk/nish` pick up a release
without anyone publishing by hand. 0.10.0 was the first version on the
registry and was published by hand, because trust can only be set on a
package that already exists.

A new `npm` job runs after `release`:

- **No token.** Each of the five packages trusts `release.yml` in this
  repository, and the job proves it is that workflow with a short-lived
  OIDC token. There is no `NPM_TOKEN` secret, and every version carries a
  provenance attestation. It is the only job that holds `id-token: write`,
  and it runs no `npm ci`.
- **The bytes the release carries.** It downloads the tarballs back from the
  GitHub release rather than packing again.
- **Platform packages first, the main package last**, so a publish that fails
  half way leaves no version of the launcher on npm without its binaries.
- **Re-runnable.** Every version already on the registry is skipped, so
  "Re-run failed jobs" finishes what a failed run started.
- **A new package fails before anything is uploaded**, naming the manual
  publish and the `npm trust` command it needs first.

Publishing 0.10.0 also broke `main` in two ways, both fixed here. The
lockfile now carries the four platform packages at 0.10.0, with integrity
hashes equal to the release tarballs, because `npm ci` refuses a lockfile
that omits a published optional dependency. And the wp12 pack-and-install
test installs with `--omit=optional`, in a directory outside the checkout,
so the "no platform package" refusal it checks is not satisfied by the
registry or by the repository's own `node_modules`.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: give a function the arena scope when only its callees allocate
entries.body:
A function with a scalar result can now bracket itself with
`nish_arena_mark` / `nish_arena_release` when the arena memory comes from
its callees rather than from its own allocations. Until now the automatic
scope needed an allocation of the function's own that flows `local`, so a
function that only called allocating helpers and kept a number, such as
Are We Fast Yet's `List.benchmark`, kept everything its callees built
until something further out released it.

The scope needs the function to be *contained*: nothing allocated during
the call can outlive it except through the return value. Either of two
proofs is enough:

- WP9's `!allocEscapes`, already propagated over every callee, which
  counts any store of an allocation into memory as an escape;
- every parameter, `this` included, is a scalar, a string, or an object
  whose fields are all scalars. Memory older than the call then has no
  slot a pointer fits in.

A new performance warning, NL9011, names a loop over such a call in a
function that still gets no scope, and says what refused it.

Measured: Storage 1000 with its manual Arena calls removed, 373 ms and
390 MB peak RSS on 0.10.0, now 167 ms and 10 MB. List 1 100000 peak RSS
drops from 50 MB to 10 MB.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: a passed bounds check proves the same index on the same array
entries.body:
A checked `a[i]` either panics or continues with `0 <= i < a.length`,
because `nish_panic_index` never returns. The bounds proof in
`self/bounds.ts` now records that fact on the path past every check it
leaves in place, so a repeat of the same index on the same array or string
carries no second check.

In Are We Fast Yet's `Permute.swap`, four checks become two: the stores
`this.v[i] = this.v[j]` and `this.v[j] = tmp` are proven by the reads
before them.

The new facts go into the existing fact families, keyed on the existing
local or property-path holders, so every existing invalidation drops them
unchanged: any call, `push` or `pop`, a store to a field named on the
path, and reassigning the index or the array. A check inside a branch
that does not dominate the repeat proves nothing past the join, and no
fact rides a loop's back-edge.

One case needed a new rule. `this.v[i] = f()` loads `this.v` before the
call and checks after it, so a store whose value makes any call records
nothing for a path holder.

Measured: Permute 1000 runs 8.9% fewer instructions (cachegrind,
339.7M to 309.5M); after `opt -O3` its swap has 2 checks instead of 3.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: keep a field array's header live across element stores
entries.body:
Array element loads and stores now carry a TBAA tag of their own,
`element <type>`, a sibling of the field tags under the same root. With
it LLVM can prove that an element store leaves a class field alone. So a
method that reads and writes `this.v[i]` keeps `this.v`, and the array's
length, live across its own stores instead of reloading both after
every one.

This is sound because an array's data block and a class object are
distinct allocations that never overlap. The places where an element store
really does write a field keep their old tags and stay untagged:

- arrays of inline records, whose element slots *are* record fields;
- `Result` payloads.

Pointer-typed elements share one `element ptr` node, the way pointer
fields already share `ptr`.

The bounds-check fail path was measured as well. `nish_panic_index` is
already `cold noreturn`, so LLVM places the fail block out of line; an
explicit branch weight measured within noise and was not kept.

Measured: after `opt -O3`, AWFY Permute's swap loads `this.v` once and
its length once (before: twice each), with exactly two bounds checks.
tests: arr_field_reload_records; the arr_field_reload structural guard in tests/run.js
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: record the shared write that denies a function purity
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: the Are We Fast Yet ports as benchmarks and regression cases
entries.body:
The seven Are We Fast Yet ports (Bounce, List, Mandelbrot, Permute,
Queens, Storage, Towers) now live in `bench/awfy/`, with their upstream
attribution and licence notices. They are corpus programs, so every
compiler change is compared against them. `node bench/run.mjs --only awfy`
times them (the median of the last 20 of 30 iterations). The `--validate`
mode, which `npm test` runs, fails if any benchmark's `verifyResult`
does. Storage no longer calls `Arena` itself: the compiler reclaims its
trees now.

`docs/wp9-optimisation.md` records 0.10.0 against main after the
arena-scope, repeated-check and element-TBAA changes, on one machine, with
the targets that were and were not met. It also profiles Queens and Towers
against the C++ port. The array header's `data` and `length` loads carry
no TBAA tag, so a class-field store forces them to be reloaded. The doc
proposes tagging them and, later, inlining fixed-length array fields.

Measured: Storage 381 → 166 ms and 390 MB → 1.7 MB peak RSS;
Permute 36.6 → 31.2 ms; Queens +5.2% and Bounce +19.2% with equal or
fewer instructions, which a loop-alignment diagnostic attributes to code
placement.
tests: node bench/run.mjs --validate --only awfy (the WP9 bench check in tests/run.js)
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: compile-time function parameters, monomorphised per callee
entries.body:
A parameter of a top-level function may now have a function type. Its argument is either a top-level function named at the call or an arrow written there, and each distinct callee is its own instantiation, keyed by template, type arguments and function arguments:

```ts
const apply = <T>(xs: T[], f: (x: T) => T): void => { ... f(xs[i]) ... };
apply(values, square);        // one specialised define, a direct call to square
apply(values, (x) => x * 3);  // a second one, calling the lifted arrow directly
```

There is no runtime function value anywhere. The parameter has no LLVM parameter and no local, the call inside the instance is a direct call, and the whole-program fixpoint sees an ordinary call edge it can prove attributes through. This is the shape wp23 §6.1 described, and the zero-cost kind WP28 §7.4 measured: a callee the checker can name, and no other kind. The `Function` Phase 0 rule and its reason are unchanged.

A name bound to a function parameter may only be called, or passed on to another function parameter. Storing, returning, comparing or collecting one is refused, and so is:
- an arrow that captures a local, `this` or an outer function parameter;
- an arrow anywhere but as a function argument;
- a function type anywhere but a top-level function's parameter;
- an argument that is not a function name or an arrow.

These are NL2334–NL2344. Each is reported once per template body, not once per instantiation. A lifted arrow is `@<enclosing>$arrow<n>` with its own `-g` subprogram. A private callee that another module's instantiation calls is `hidden`, not `internal`. No interop sidecar ever describes a function-argument instance.

This is the construct `parallelMapInto` and `parallelReduce` take their body through (wp29 P1).
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: fail the suite when a benchmark executes more instructions than its baseline
entries.body:
Wall time on a VM is noisier than a codegen regression of a few
percent, so `npm test` now counts the instructions each of the 14
benchmark programs executes (the seven `bench/*.ts` programs and the
seven Are We Fast Yet ports) under cachegrind. It fails when any count
rises more than 0.1% above `bench/instructions.json`.

`node bench/run.mjs --instructions` builds the programs exactly as the
timing mode does and prints each count against the baseline. `--check`
exits 1 on a regression, and `--update` rewrites the baseline. The count
covers the whole process, so everything about it that varies between
hosts is pinned. The child's environment holds only `GLIBC_TUNABLES`,
which sends every x86-64 host to glibc's SSE2 `memcpy`/`memset`; left
alone, their choice varied strbuild's count by 30%. Programs run as
`./name` from their own directory. After pinning, the largest residual
between hosts measured is 0.006%.

The check is a counted skip off linux-x64, and when valgrind or clang is
missing. CI's Linux test row installs valgrind.
metrics: whole check about 16 s; switching off the bounds prover raises Queens by 0.858% and fails it
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: parallelMapInto and parallelReduce from nish/threads
entries.body:
Two data-parallel calls arrive in `nish/threads`: `parallelMapInto(src, dst, f)` writes `f(src[i])` into `dst[i]`, and `parallelReduce(src, f, identity)` folds `src` with `f`. Both run across the machine's cores on the existing `nish_parallel_range` partitioner. They are the first use of compile-time function parameters: `f` is a named function or an arrow, and it is monomorphised into the call rather than passed as a value.

`std/threads.ts` is ordinary Nish whose bodies are the sequential meaning, so the same file runs unchanged under Node. Importing it implies `--threads`, which makes the arena thread-local. A program that does not import it compiles byte for byte as before.

Race freedom is judged at the call from the whole-program facts, and each refusal names what it found:

- NL2345: `f` writes memory its caller can see, naming the store or the callee that makes it; `console.log` counts.
- NL2346: `f` allocates. This is strict for now; the next stage relaxes it.
- NL2347: `dst` is reachable from an element of `src`, naming the field path.
- NL2348: the result is not a number, `boolean` or enum.
- NL2349 and NL2350: a reduce arrow uses a non-associative operator, or an identity that does not match its operator.

A bounds check, an integer division or a `panic` inside `f` is not a write, so bodies that contain them are accepted.

A reduce is deterministic. It splits the input into at most 64 blocks of 2^20 elements (`BLOCK`), folds each from the identity, and combines the partial results in order. It does the same on one thread, so an `f64` sum has the same bits on any core count and under Node. A map divides its range by `GRAIN` (2^20 elements, independent of `BLOCK`), so a short array runs as the plain loop on the calling thread.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: allocating parallel bodies, a cost-sized grain and the NL9012 warning
entries.body:
A `parallelMapInto` body may now allocate. Before, any allocation in the function passed as `f` was refused.

- **When an allocating body is admitted.** Nothing it allocates escapes, it returns a scalar, and it neither reads nor moves the `Arena`. The body then gets an arena scope of its own: it marks the arena on entry and releases it before returning, so every element's garbage is recycled at once.
- **Why that is sound.** Importing `nish/threads` makes the arena thread-local, so the mark and release name the arena of whichever thread runs the element.
- **The warning.** An allocating body compiles with performance warning NL9012, which says what the recycling costs. It honours `--no-warn-performance` and `--json`. (NL9011 was already the arena-loop warning.)
- **New refusals.** NL2351 refuses a body that reads or moves the arena. NL2352 refuses one whose allocation is stored into memory, and names the site.
- **A retired code.** NL2346, the old blanket refusal, is retired.

A map's grain is now sized from a static estimate of one element's cost, `2^22 / cost(f)`, in place of a fixed 2^20 elements.

- **How the cost is estimated.** It counts nodes, calls and allocations. A loop counts as its trip count when its header is written in literals, and as 64 trips otherwise.
- **Short maps.** A map no longer than its grain calls its chunk loop directly, which LLVM inlines, so a short map costs about what the plain loop does.
- **Reduce is unchanged.** Its blocking, and therefore its answer's bits, are exactly as before.

Measured with `node bench/run.mjs` on 4 cores, against the plain loop:

| kernel | speedup |
|---|---|
| compute kernel | 3.71x |
| partitioned n-body | 3.49x |
| allocating kernel (peak memory unchanged) | 2.23x |
| 8-element map | 0.97x, within noise |

The `par_*` kernels stay out of the instruction-count gate: valgrind serialises threads, so their counts would depend on scheduling.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: give array header loads and stores their own TBAA subtree
entries.body:
Every load and store of an array header's `len`, `cap` or `data` now
carries a `!tbaa` tag in an `array header` subtree of its own. It sits
under the same root as the class-field paths and the element subtree,
so LLVM knows that a class-field store cannot write an array's header.
Until now every field store forced the header to be reloaded. In AWFY
Towers' inlined `moveTopDisk`, `opt -O3` now loads the header's length
and data pointer once per move rather than three times each, and one
bounds-check compare folds away with the reload.

The tag is sound because every write of a header's bytes either
carries it or sits behind a call. All header accesses in the compiler
go through `headerFieldPointer` in `self/emit_arrays.ts`. The runtime's
C writers (`nish_array_grow`, `nish_alloc_array`, `nish_readdir`,
argv) are reached only through calls, and carry clang's own TBAA root
under LTO. Parallel regions write no shared header. The full argument
is in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`.

In the stripped speed-profile binary on one Intel host, Towers' wall
time is 6.8% slower. The cause is a fused compare-and-branch that now
straddles a 32-byte boundary (the JCC erratum), not extra work: linked
with branch padding, the same IR runs 11% faster than before.
metrics: Towers executes 11.2% fewer instructions (263,067,587 to 233,554,787); the other 13 benchmarks are unchanged

entries.title: reclaim a loop iteration's temporaries when nothing outlives the pass
entries.body:
A loop whose pass drops everything it allocates now gets an arena scope
of its own. The bump position is read at the top of the body, and every
edge that leaves the pass rewinds to it: the back-edge, `continue`,
`break`, and a `return`, which releases the outermost scope open. This
applies in a function of any return type. A pointer-returning function
never had a scope, so #216's `summarise(rounds): Box`, which drops one
list per pass, kept every pass's list until its caller released. Its
peak resident set is now flat from 100 rounds to 4000.

A pass is scoped when nothing it allocates, itself or through a callee,
is reachable afterwards except through a number, a `boolean` or an
`enum`:
- no allocation of the pass is stored into memory, by the body or by
  any callee;
- an outer local that can hold a pointer is assigned only values older
  than the pass;
- a `return` answers a scalar or an older value;
- the function neither calls `Arena.mark`/`release`/`reset` nor reaches
  a callee that releases or resets;
- and the pass allocates something.

The mark is read inline from `@nish_arena`. The release rewinds `off`
when `buf` is unchanged, and calls `nish_arena_release` only when the
pass pushed a chunk.

An element of an array whose elements are inline is the address of a
slot in that array, and is now followed as the array. Before, a function
could store `xs[i]` into its parameter's object, take the function scope
and release the block it pointed into: `mem_loop_scope_interior` printed
`8 16` where the answer is `49 98`.

NL9011 now fires in a function of any return type, and only where
neither a pass scope nor a function scope reclaims the call's memory.
It names what refused each scope, and it stays silent under `Arena`
control.
metrics: #216 probe 66,600 KB -> 1,448 KB at 4000 rounds; 10^8-pass loop 1.6-16.4 s -> 0.23 s; one small array per pass over 100k passes -0.6% instructions
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: fingerprints and stored hashes in StringMap
entries.body:
The compiler's own string-keyed map, `StringMap` in `self/map.ts`, now uses the layout that `docs/wp32-map.md` chose for the global `Map`.

- **Slots.** Each bucket is a packed `u32`: an 8-bit fingerprint (the top of the FNV-1a hash) above a 24-bit entry index plus one.
- **Stored hashes.** Every entry stores its full hash.
- **Probing.** A probe reads an entry only when the fingerprint matches, and compares the stored hash before the string.
- **Growth** re-files buckets from the stored hashes and never hashes a key again.
- **`StringSet.add`** is one probe instead of a lookup followed by an insert.
- **Unchanged:** iteration order and the public API. The compiler's output is byte-identical: `nish-cmp` shows no moved program, and the bootstrap reaches its fixed point.

On compiling itself, the compiler is not measurably faster: wall time is within noise, instructions are +0.04%, and peak RSS is +0.4% for the stored hashes. The symbol tables are too small for the layout's gains to show. What the compiler gets is the WP32 layout, with its invariants pinned by the support oracle:
- a fingerprint that matches while the hash differs;
- a real FNV-1a collision;
- growth to 2^18 buckets;
- the slot packing at both ends of its 24-bit index field.
metrics: stage-2 compile of self/compile.ts, median 474/472/479 ms before vs 490/472/460 ms after; +0.04% instructions; +0.4% peak RSS
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: prove an index in range from what every call site guarantees
entries.body:
A new whole-program pass, `self/ranges.ts`, runs `self/bounds.ts`'s
proof a second time once every body has been checked. This time it
knows two things the per-body pass cannot: what each callee can do to a
caller's facts, and what every call site of a function proves about its
parameters.

**Call summaries.** A callee that resizes no array keeps the caller's
length facts alive across the call. A function loses its summary if it
calls a builtin handed an array or object (`push`, `pop`), `Arena`, a
foreign function or an instantiation, or if it stores to a field named
`length`.

**Entry facts.** These are floors, upper bounds and `below`/`atMost`
relations on a parameter or on a path read off it. They are joined over
every call site, and a later argument that writes an earlier one's
local voids what that earlier argument carried. Recursion is a fixpoint
capped at 64 rounds; past the cap the pass keeps no entry fact at all.
A decrement keeps the upper bounds and loses the lower ones.

**Who takes entry facts.** Only a function every call of which is
visible. `hostVisible` in the new `self/visibility.ts` decides this from
the declaration and the build mode. A `--link` build with a native
profile and triple, no `--emit-header`/`--emit-dts`/`--emit-napi` and
no `declare function` is its own final link: the executable holds only
the program's modules and the runtime. There, `export` means only
"importable", and exported functions and methods take entry facts. Every
other build is open, and the entry point always is. A closed build's
`.ll` files belong to that executable and are not objects for another
link.

In `--link` builds the pass now walks every exported function, and
`self/` exports nearly all of them. Compiling `self/` costs +4.7%
instructions (+6.4% CPU, +4.4% peak RSS), and the AWFY harness +6.7%
(about 0.4 ms). A narrower candidate test is planned as a follow-up.
Builds without `--link` pay only the base pass (+2.6%).
metrics: AWFY Permute -42.5% instructions (286,429,789 -> 164,701,789), -53% wall; Towers -5.6%, Storage -3.2% instructions; 16 of self/'s NL9007 warnings retracted

entries.title: store a fixed-length array field inside its object
entries.body:
A class field `f: T[]` that provably only ever holds a fresh array of a
known length, and whose array is never used as a value, is now laid out
inside its object. The `nish_array` header and K element slots replace
the pointer, and the header's `data` points at the slots from `new` on.
`this.f[i]` becomes a bounds check on `len` and one load at a constant
offset from `this`, with no field pointer and no `data` load first.
Reference semantics are unchanged.

A field qualifies only if all of these hold, over every module:
- every assignment is a fresh array of a literal length: a literal,
  `new Array<T>(n)`, or a top-level function proven to return one, like
  AWFY Queens' `filledBooleans(8)`. K is the largest such length, and
  the header keeps `len`;
- `x.f` is only ever indexed or asked for `.length`;
- no element access's index or stored value can reach an assignment to
  the field;
- the class is not host-visible;
- the build shares no layouts: no header, dts, napi, wasm or
  `declare function`;
- the class is plain, and the slots fit in 256 bytes.

A store into an inline field now counts as a write through the receiver,
so `readonly` is no longer inferred on it. Header accesses still go
through the tagged helpers, and inline members stay out of the class's
struct path.

An array assigned from a call is built and then copied into the slots.
A field reassigned that way and read only a few times per assignment is
slower (+85-118% in a microbenchmark); fields read dozens of times or
more per assignment are faster, and direct assignments are faster at
every size.
metrics: AWFY wall Permute -15.2%, Towers -15.9%, Queens -5.4%; instructions Queens -16.8%, Permute -7.5%, Towers -4.2%; Queens.getRowColumn 12 loads -> 6 after opt -O3
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: carry the licence of every third-party copy, and make agents keep it
entries.body:
An audit of the tree found code copied from three upstreams without the
notice their licences require. One of them ships in the npm package.

- `runtime/runtime.c`'s shortest round-trip float formatting is adapted
  from Ryu (`ryu/d2s.c`, `ryu/common.h`, Copyright 2018 Ulf Adams),
  which is dual-licensed Apache-2.0 or BSL-1.0. This repository takes
  BSL-1.0, which exempts compiled object code: neither `nish` nor a
  program it links needs a notice. The block now carries the notice,
  and `runtime/LICENSE-ryu` ships with `runtime/` in every package and
  release tarball.
- `bench/nbody.*`, `examples/nbody.ts` and `bench/spectral.*` are
  adapted from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game n-body and
  spectral-norm programs (Revised BSD). They now carry its notice, with
  the licence in `bench/LICENSE-benchmarksgame.md`.
- Twelve tests and cookbook snippets copy parts of the Are We Fast Yet
  ports (SOM, MIT). Each now carries the MIT notice and is listed in
  `bench/awfy/LICENSE.md`.

`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` lists every third-party file and its licence.
The README's licence section points at it. A new
`.claude/licensing.md`, referenced from `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` and
`.claude/orientation.md`, gives every contributor and agent the rule:
- what counts as a copy;
- the notice and licence text a copy keeps, in the repository and in the
  package when it ships;
- the MIT-compatible licences allowed;
- the sources never to take code from: GPL-family, Rosetta Code, Stack
  Overflow, Project Euler, unlicensed.

`node tests/run.js third-party-licence` holds the list, the files and
the packages to each other in both directions.
metrics: IR unchanged apart from !dbg line numbers; all 18 instruction counts +0.000%
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: Map.get, typed V | undefined and narrowed as TypeScript does
entries.body:
`m.get(k)` on the global `Map` now type-checks as it does under `tsc --strict`. Its type is `V | undefined`, a *maybe*, that is narrowed by `!== undefined` / `=== undefined` or collapsed by `??`, and every `get` is exactly one probe.

**Where a maybe may appear.** The three places `docs/wp32-map.md` §3.2 decides:
- the initialiser of a `const` (unannotated, or annotated `V | undefined`);
- the left operand of `??`;
- an operand of `=== undefined` / `!== undefined`.

Everywhere else it is refused with a code for the place and a message that names the fix (NL2361–NL2369): a `let` (annotated or not), an argument, a `return`, a field, an element, a template hole, another operator's operand, and a `const` annotated `V`.

**Narrowing** reuses the nullable rules, with `undefined` in place of `null`. `undefined` stays refused everywhere else.

**`??`** parses with TypeScript's precedence: at the level of `||`, left associative. Mixing it with `||`/`&&` without parentheses is one syntax error, as TS5076 is. Its default must be `V` (NL2370, NL2371). For a nullable `V` it also replaces a stored `null`. A `??` whose left operand is not a maybe is still refused (NL1048).

**Lowering: two SSA values and no memory.** The found bit is the probe's answer, and the value is read only on the found edge. `m.get(k) ?? d` is the probe, a branch and a `phi`, so `d` runs only when the key is missing, as in JavaScript. Under `-g` a maybe `const` is described with `llvm.dbg.value`.

**Also fixed:** a miscompile found while building this, where `m.set(k, m.get(k) ?? new Node(...))` put the `Node` on the stack. The retired "not supported yet" refusal, NL2357, keeps its number reserved.
metrics: a word count spelled `m.set(w, (m.get(w) ?? 0) + 1)` prints Node's counts in insertion order, byte for byte; 33 `get`s across the goldens make 33 probes
